name: THE ALL HOT AND COLLARD BURGER

recipe.history:
Collard greens are among the oldest cultivated vegetables in human history, belonging to the Brassica oleracea species alongside cabbage, kale, and broccoli. They have been grown and eaten in the Mediterranean basin for at least two thousand years — ancient Greeks and Romans prized them for their medicinal as well as culinary properties, and Apicius, the first-century Roman cookbook, includes recipes for braised greens similar to collards. The plant's ability to thrive in poor soil and cool climates made it a staple crop wherever people needed to grow food from difficult land. In Africa, particularly in the region of West and Central Africa, varieties of the same Brassica family were cultivated for centuries, and when enslaved Africans were forcibly transported to the Americas beginning in the sixteenth century, they carried knowledge of these greens with them. In the American South, collard greens became deeply embedded in the food culture of African-Americans and poor white Southerners alike — slow-cooked in a pot with a ham hock or salt pork, the pot liquor (the savory, nutrient-rich cooking liquid) valued as much as the greens themselves. Collards braised low and slow until silky, tender, and deeply flavored with smoky pork became one of the foundational dishes of American Southern cuisine.

Collard greens moved into the mainstream American culinary conversation as part of the broader recognition of Southern food as a serious and sophisticated regional cuisine. Chefs like Sean Brock, Edna Lewis, and later Michael Twitty worked to reclaim and recontextualize Southern food within its full historical and cultural complexity, including the African and African-American roots that had been systematically undervalued. Collards on a burger arrived naturally from this conversation — as Southern-inspired restaurants began applying slow-cooked, deeply seasoned greens to sandwiches and burgers, recognizing that braised collards do for a beef patty what sauerkraut does for a frankfurter: they provide the acidic, complex, savory counterweight that makes meat taste more fully itself. Spiced with hot sauce, finished with apple cider vinegar, and layered against sharp cheese and sweet onion, collard greens become one of the most compelling burger toppings in the American regional tradition.

My grandmother braised collard greens every Sunday of my childhood from roughly November through March, and her technique was the opposite of anything fast or fashionable: a huge pot, a ham hock submerged in water, low heat for hours until the greens were olive-dark and collapsing, the pot liquor reduced to a glossy, smoky, salty broth that she served in a cup alongside the greens as a kind of restorative. I ate those greens happily as a child and then spent most of my twenties avoiding them — the association with slow Sunday afternoons and the smell of long-cooked pork felt too heavy, too removed from the city life I was trying to build. It took a lunch at a tiny soul food counter in Memphis to bring me back: collards braised with vinegar and hot sauce, still silky but lifted by acid, piled on a griddled patty on a squishy bun. I thought about my grandmother's pot liquor the whole drive home and called her that evening to ask for the recipe.

You will cook this patty to medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, 54 to 57 degrees Celsius — because the contrast between the hot, slow-cooked greens and the pink, yielding interior of a properly cooked patty is exactly the point of this burger. The acidity and depth of braised collards need something rich and uncomplicated at their center to anchor them. A well-done patty is too dry, too dense, too assertive in its own way — it competes with the greens for dominance. A medium-rare patty is the quiet, confident center that lets the collards do their work without a fight. Medium rare is not just a preference here; it is the structural logic of the dish.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
1 large bunch collard greens (about 1 lb), stems removed, leaves roughly chopped
4 oz smoked bacon or salt pork, cut into lardons
Salt and black pepper to taste
4 oz sharp yellow cheddar, freshly grated
instructions: 1. Braise the collard greens: In a wide, heavy pot or Dutch oven over medium heat, render bacon lardons until fat is released and bacon is crispy. Remove bacon and set aside, leaving fat in the pot. Add onion to bacon fat and cook over medium heat 8 minutes until softened and golden. Add garlic and red pepper flakes; cook 1 minute. Add collard greens in batches, stirring as they wilt to make room for more. Once all greens are in the pot, add chicken stock, apple cider vinegar, hot sauce, and sugar. Stir well. Bring to a simmer, cover, and cook over low heat for 45 minutes to 1 hour, stirring occasionally, until greens are very tender and silky. Return bacon lardons to the pot. Season generously with salt and pepper. Keep warm.

2. Make the pimento cheese: Combine grated cheddar, cream cheese, mayonnaise, pimentos, cayenne, and garlic powder in a bowl. Mix well with a fork until creamy and well combined. Season with salt and pepper. Refrigerate until needed.

3. Make the cornbread bun dough: Dissolve yeast and sugar in warm buttermilk and water in a stand mixer bowl. Let bloom 5 minutes. Add egg, melted butter, salt, cornmeal, and all-purpose flour. Mix with dough hook on medium speed 7 minutes until smooth and slightly sticky. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover, and rise 1 hour until doubled.

4. Divide dough into 4 balls, flatten into bun rounds on a parchment-lined sheet, cover, and proof 40 minutes. Preheat oven to 375°F. Brush with egg wash and bake 15–17 minutes until golden. Cool on a rack.

5. Form the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 portions (about 6 oz each). Form into patties 3/4 inch thick with a thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt, black pepper, smoked paprika, and cayenne.

6. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Sear patties undisturbed 3 minutes. Flip, place a slice of pepper jack cheese on each, and cook 2–3 more minutes. Check internal temperature — pull at 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest 3 minutes.
7. Toast bun halves cut-side down in the skillet 60 seconds.

8. Assemble: Spread pimento cheese generously on the bottom bun. Add a generous heap of braised collard greens with some of the pot liquor. Place the medium-rare, cheese-topped patty on top. Add bread-and-butter pickles. Finish with flaky sea salt and the top bun. Serve immediately.
